The results show that changes in accessibility determine a modal shift from private transport to MaaS; the new hospital, with more employees, determines an increase in residents and employment; the land prices influence the spatial distribution of the population. These first findings can be replicated analytically using simple pen-and-paper computations and can be extended to the logistics component. They could offer useful support for land-use and transport planners, although parameter calibration and model validation against real-world case studies are still required.

title: Design Principles for Data-Centric Semantic Interoperability in IoT: The IoTTD Ontology
abstract: The increasing heterogeneity of Internet of Things (IoT) devices continues to challenge semantic interoperability across heterogeneous platforms and application domains. Although numerous IoT ontologies and standards have been proposed, many emphasize comprehensive semantic modeling, even in scenarios where only interoperable device data exchange is required, resulting in increased complexity, domain specificity, and limited adoption for generic device data exchange. This paper proposes a data-centric design approach for semantic interoperability based on a set of design principles specifically developed for the semantic representation of IoT device data. Guided by these principles, we introduce IoT Things&rsquo; Description (IoTTD), a lightweight OWL ontology that provides a standardized semantic representation for heterogeneous IoT device data. Rather than modeling the complete conceptual space of IoT systems, IoTTD focuses exclusively on the common semantic interface required for interoperable device data exchange. The ontology enables bidirectional semantic data sharing and supports generic SPARQL-based access without requiring prior knowledge of the IoTTD ontology&rsquo;s structure or content. IoTTD and the proposed design approach are evaluated through structural comparison with representative IoT ontologies, logical consistency verification using HermiT reasoning, semantic annotation examples, and representative application scenarios. The results demonstrate that IoTTD achieves substantially lower structural complexity while preserving the semantic capabilities required for interoperable IoT device data representation. The proposed design principles, together with their implementation in IoTTD, provide the foundation for lightweight semantic interoperability and can serve as a semantic basis for interoperable IoT Knowledge Graphs and Semantic Web applications.

title: Complementary Global&ndash;Local Feature Fusion and Ensemble Refinement for Facial-Expression Recognition on FER2013
abstract: Facial-expression recognition (FER) on FER2013 remains challenging because of low-resolution images, class imbalance, and label ambiguity. This study presents a global&ndash;local feature-fusion framework that integrates complementary representations with validation-based ensemble refinement. A frozen DINOv2 ViT-Base captures global facial semantics, while EfficientNetB3 extracts complementary local texture features. Their fused representation is used for seven-class facial-expression classification. The classification head is first trained with targeted feature-space SMOTE, and the EfficientNetB3 branch is then partially fine-tuned. Five-view test-time augmentation (TTA) is further incorporated at inference, together with an independently trained ConvNeXt-Tiny branch to provide additional architectural diversity. Ensemble weights are selected using a held-out validation set, while the test partition is reserved for final evaluation. On the 7178-image FER2013 test partition, the resulting ensemble achieves 76.51% accuracy, 75.77% macro F1, 76.32% weighted F1, 0.7158 Cohen&rsquo;s kappa, and 0.9574 macro ROC AUC. The results demonstrate the potential of combining complementary global&ndash;local representations, inference augmentation, and ensemble refinement for facial-expression recognition on FER2013.

title: Reactance-Aware Recursive Alignment for Human&ndash;AI Translation: Modeling Translator Agency and Task-Specific Critical Automation Capability
abstract: Professional translators may resist highly directive AI assistance when it threatens perceived autonomy, authorship, and control. This study introduces the Recursive Control and Alignment Protocol (ReCAP), a reactance-aware framework for interactive machine translation. ReCAP combines a reactance-potential model with a recursive loop of Intent Inference, Reactance-Guided Generation, and Critical Feedback Integration. Its Adversarial Reactance Minimization objective balances translation quality against estimated autonomy costs, and the task-specific Critical Automation Capability Index (CACI) provides an exploratory behavioral summary of critical engagement. In an evaluation with 156 professional translators across four English-based bidirectional language-pair settings, ReCAP achieved a mean COMET &times; 100 score of 36.8, 2.8 points above QE-guided MT (34.0), the strongest baseline, across five seed-matched runs per method&ndash;language-pair configuration. Mixed-effects estimates showed lower reported reactance for ReCAP than QE-guided MT (&beta; = &minus;0.55, 95% CI [&minus;0.71, &minus;0.39]) and higher exploratory CACI scores than CHORUS (&beta; = 0.64, 95% CI [0.44, 0.84]). Post hoc CACI checks remained task-specific and exploratory. These findings support a run-level translation-quality advantage and task-specific human-outcome associations under the evaluated conditions.

title: Personal Data Management System Architectures: A Systematic Review
abstract: The increase in personal data generation and the evolving landscape of digital information management necessitate robust and secure software architectures for personal data management systems. This systematic literature review examines the architectures proposed for such systems, classifying them as centralized, decentralized, or hybrid. The classification criterion is applied to the evidence the studies report rather than to the label its authors adopt. It separates the custody of the data from the coordination of its processing, because two systems that describe themselves as decentralized distribute only the former. The review analyzes 15 studies, retrieved from three databases, one search engine, and other sources, published between January 2014 and February 2026, examining the methodologies, technologies, and architectural strategies employed in personal data management systems. The review highlights the strengths and limitations of different software architectures in terms of scalability, security, and compliance with the European Union&rsquo;s General Data Protection Regulation, a regulatory regime addressed explicitly by several of the reviewed architecture studies. Key findings reveal a significant gap in the current literature. No shared benchmark or dataset appears in the corpus. The evidence therefore supports qualitative but not empirical comparison between architectural approaches.

title: A Lightweight Fine-Grained Malicious Request Detection Model Towards Smart Grid Cloud Services
abstract: To address the challenges in malicious request detection in smart grid cloud service scenarios, including the difficulty of effectively capturing the semantic relationships within payloads, the large parameter scale and high inference costs of pre-trained language models, an efficient and relatively lightweight, fine-grained malicious request detection model named DFEF-Net (DistilBERT-based FiLM-enhanced Expert Feature Network, DFEF-Net) is proposed. First, the model is based on the lightweight pre-trained language model DistilBERT and constructs 14-dimensional expert-based features to characterize the statistical information of request payloads, so as to strengthen its ability to represent request structural features and anomalous patterns. Second, the feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) mechanism is introduced to adaptively modulate deep semantic features, effectively fusing semantic features with structural features. Finally, experiments on the proposed scheme are conducted on four public Web/HTTP attack datasets (HttpParams, HTTP CSIC 2010, FWAF, and SecureAI-SE). On these benchmarks, DFEF-Net achieves over 99% accuracy in binary attack detection on all four datasets. In multi-class attack identification, DFEF-Net reaches 99.27% macro-F1 on HttpParams and 97.00% on SecureAI-SE. RoBERTa slightly surpasses it on SecureAI-SE but drops to 59.53% macro-F1 on HttpParams, whereas DFEF-Net maintains balanced recognition across both datasets. Per-class analysis and multi-seed results further show relatively consistent fine-grained recognition across attack categories. Compared with BERT-based baseline models, DFEF-Net reduces model parameter count by approximately 39%, model size by 39%, FLOPs by 50%, and per-request inference latency by approximately 40&ndash;60% under the evaluated protocol. Consequently, the proposed approach offers a favorable trade-off among detection performance, computational cost, and fine-grained attack identification on the evaluated public Web/HTTP benchmarks, providing an efficient algorithmic basis for future evaluation in smart grid cloud services, while domain-specific validation on real smart-grid traffic remains necessary.

title: Quantifying the Impact of Construction Vessel Interference on Port Operations: An Agent-Based Simulation and Regression Analysis Framework
abstract: Port infrastructure development increasingly brings construction vessels into conflict with commercial shipping, yet quantitative assessments of such interference remain scarce. This study proposes a framework to quantify the impact of construction vessel activities on port operational efficiency. Three categories of construction vessels&mdash;channel-crossing, channel-occupying, and berth-occupying&mdash;are identified and modelled using agent-based simulation in AnyLogic. A virtual berth concept is introduced to represent construction vessel resource occupation, and the model is calibrated using data from a case-study port. Simulation outputs across varying traffic demand and construction vessel configurations are analyzed through multiple regression to derive quantitative estimates of interference. The results show that the three categories impose distinctly different levels of impact. Channel-occupying vessels have the most substantial effect, equivalent to approximately 8&ndash;10 commercial vessels at half the baseline demand level and 30&ndash;33 at three times the baseline level. Berth-occupying vessels correspond to roughly 2&ndash;4 and 20&ndash;22 commercial vessels, respectively, while channel-crossing vessels correspond to approximately 1.5&ndash;2.5 and 19&ndash;22. The framework is transferable to other port settings and provides a quantitative basis for prioritizing mitigation measures and informing construction scheduling.

title: DigiHerit: Enhancing Cultural Heritage Education Through Gamified Mobile Exploration
abstract: Digital technologies can provide alternative forms of access to cultural heritage sites that are physically restricted or unavailable to the public; however, their effective transformation into meaningful educational experiences requires the coordination of documentation, spatial representation, interpretation, interaction, and engagement. This study presents DigiHerit, a mobile gamified application developed for the digitally reconstructed Lassani Mansion in Kozani, Greece, and uses its implementation as the empirical basis for proposing a case-derived methodological framework for access-restricted architectural heritage. The implemented workflow combined spatial documentation, three-dimensional reconstruction and optimization, real-time application development, educational content integration, gamification, and user evaluation. Through retrospective analysis of the development process, seven interconnected methodological stages were identified, with Spatial Interpretation introduced as an explicit link between documentation and subsequent reconstruction and experience-design decisions. User evaluation with 30 participants suggests positive perceptions of digital access, engagement, learning, and exploration, while also identifying areas for improvement in navigation and content delivery. The study demonstrates how a case-specific technical workflow can inform a broader design methodology without prescribing particular technologies. The resulting framework is proposed as a case-derived structure for further prospective testing and refinement across different access-restricted heritage contexts and emerging modes of digital experience.

title: A Pose Landmark-Based Lightweight Human Fall-Detection Framework Using Spatiotemporal Features
abstract: In today&rsquo;s society, with its rapidly growing aging population, automated lightweight human fall detection has become very important. We present a lightweight human fall-detection framework based on pose landmarks and dynamic spatiotemporal motion features. The proposed system integrates YOLO12n and MediaPipe to detect human regions and extract pose landmarks from video sequences. The system incorporates a traceability information panel that visualizes the effects of different features on the classification of a frame as either a fall or an Activity of Daily Living (ADL) event. We introduce four override conditions, namely Head Position Override, Aspect Ratio Override, Vertical Leg Override, and Leg Alignment Override, to suppress false positives caused by ADL events such as bending, sleeping, picking up objects from the ground, and performing exercises. In addition, we utilize seven criteria, namely body angle, vertical drop, height ratio, angle change, knee-ankle vertical distance, vertical velocity, and head proximity to the ground, to distinguish fall events from ADL events effectively. We perform temporal validation of a fall event by confirming at least two consecutive fall frames to further reduce false positives. To evaluate the proposed method, we used two datasets, namely GMDCSA-24 and URFD. The proposed system achieved accuracy values of 90.63% and 88.57% on the GMDCSA-24 and URFD datasets, respectively.

title: Benchmarking Named Entity Recognition for Low-Resource Tarifit Berber: A Comparative Evaluation of Traditional, Neural, Transformer-Based, and Span-Based Models
abstract: Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a fundamental Natural Language Processing task, yet low-resource languages such as Tarifit Berber remain critically underexplored. This study introduces the first standardized and reproducible benchmark for Tarifit NER, addressing the lack of publicly available annotated corpora and unified evaluation protocols. A manually annotated corpus was developed using the IOB2 scheme, covering nine entity categories, and subjected to rigorous quality-assurance procedures, including data-leakage detection and out-of-vocabulary (OOV) analysis. Ten representative architectures were evaluated under an identical protocol, spanning traditional statistical models (CRF), neural sequence-labeling models (BiLSTM-CRF), multilingual Transformer models (mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa, RemBERT, LUKE), Arabic-oriented pretrained models (AraBERT, MARBERT, DarijaBERT), and the span-based GLiNER approach. Evaluation combined entity- and token-level metrics, category-wise analysis, lexical robustness across known, rare, and OOV entities, and bootstrap-based statistical reliability analysis. Results show that Transformer models consistently outperform traditional statistical and neural sequence-labeling models, with mBERT achieving the highest entity-level F1 score (95.76%), followed by MARBERT, DarijaBERT, and RemBERT. Location and Date were the most challenging categories, while GLiNER performed substantially worse under strict exact-match evaluation. These findings establish a reliable benchmark for Tarifit NER and provide a reusable foundation for future research in Amazigh and multilingual NLP.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Verification and Validation of Safety-Critical Systems: A Bibliometric Science-Mapping Study and an Assurance-Level Framework (AVAF) (2016&ndash;2026)
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and formal verification and validation (V&amp;V) are two of the most consequential areas in safety-critical systems engineering, and they interact in a dual way: AI is increasingly used to support V&amp;V, while V&amp;V is increasingly applied to certify AI components whose high-dimensional and emergent behaviors resist classical methods. This study provides one of the first comprehensive bibliometric and science-mapping analyses of AI-assisted V&amp;V for safety-critical systems over 2016&ndash;2026, combining, for the first time, Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection into a single PRISMA 2020-compliant corpus of 425 documents. Descriptive bibliometrics, keyword co-occurrence and thematic mapping, trend-topic detection, and logistic lifecycle modelling reveal a field growing at 21.8% annually, mobilizing 1249 authors across 54 countries and organized into four thematic communities, formal verification with machine learning, model checking with agentic AI and large language models, and AI-driven runtime monitoring of cyber-physical systems, with large language models, theorem proving, and AI-systems verification as the youngest themes. Findings are situated against emerging AI-governance regimes, including the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, the United States NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and ISO/IEC 42001. Beyond mapping, the study contributes the AI-Verification Assurance Framework (AVAF), a three-layer instrument that codes each study by verification direction, method, and property, grades the assurance it demonstrates on an A0&ndash;A4 scale, and maps it to certification regimes; AVAF is calibrated and pilot-tested on a stratified, subsample (intra-coder test&ndash;retest Cohen&rsquo;s &kappa; = 0.84). Its application reveals a certifiability gap: assurance concentrates in bounded-formal and statistical tiers, and no study in the coded calibration subsample attains a complete formal guarantee over a realistic model or certifiable, tool-qualified evidence (A4). The paper closes with a six-point research agenda on the certification, scalability, and multi-domain transfer of AI-assisted verification.

title: Q-Conditioning and Q-Gating: Metadata-Driven Attention Mechanisms for Medical Vision Transformers
abstract: Background: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated efficacy in visual recognition tasks through global dependency modeling via self-attention. However, standard ViT architectures lack native mechanisms for integrating external clinical metadata (e.g., patient demographics, lesion characteristics, image quality indicators) into the visual processing pipeline, limiting their utility in multi-modal diagnostic scenarios. Methods: We propose two novel attention mechanisms: Q-Conditioning and Q-Gating, designed for efficient metadata fusion within the transformer framework. In Q-Conditioning, metadata is projected into the query space and added to the query vector, guiding attention toward contextually relevant regions during early computation. In Q-Gating, a learned gate modulates computed attention scores, enabling soft, differentiable control over token interactions. We further introduce a hybrid attention framework wherein standard, Q-Conditioning, and Q-Gating heads coexist within the same model. Results: We evaluated our approach on four medical imaging benchmarks (PAD-UFES-20, TissueNet, PH2, and NDB-UFES). Specific configurations, particularly Q-Gating and hybrid variants (e.g., QC_QG, QG_S), achieved &gt;95.5% accuracy on PAD-UFES-20 and &gt;92% average score on PH2, significantly outperforming image-only baseline models (p&lt;0.001). On TissueNet, where auxiliary inputs consist of PhikonV2 foundation-model embeddings rather than raw clinical metadata, all configurations exceeded 99% accuracy; however, we note that these gains are substantially attributable to the pretrained encoder and are reported separately from the primary clinical-metadata claims. Attention concentration metrics, encompassing both theoretical conditional entropy reduction and empirical absolute entropy dispersion, correlated strongly with diagnostic performance gains (&rho;=0.89), indicating improved focus on diagnostically salient regions while avoiding spurious attention collapse. Conclusions: Metadata-aware attention mechanisms enhance both performance and interpretability in domains where auxiliary information is critical. This work provides a scalable extension to ViTs that supports multi-input modeling while preserving architectural integrity and computational efficiency.

title: Mobility and Logistics as a Service for Healthcare (MLaaS4H): Transport Planning Processes for Enhancing Sustainable People Mobility to Healthcare Facilities
abstract: Rapid urbanisation poses increasingly complex sustainability challenges, while transport systems remain essential for enabling people and businesses to conduct daily activities and access critical services. This study investigates the interactions between passenger and freight mobility and the healthcare sector and proposes Mobility and Logistics as a Service for Healthcare (MLaaS4H), an integrated framework for the sustainable planning of healthcare-related mobility and logistics. The framework aims to support decision-making and service design by combining advanced transport system models (TSMs) with emerging information and communication technologies (e-ICTs), thereby improving accessibility to healthcare facilities and the efficiency of service provision. The proposed planning process comprises two complementary paths. The external path connects the spatial, temporal, and deepening dimensions of transport and healthcare planning, whereas the internal path adopts the Logical Framework Approach (LFA) to establish a transparent causal chain linking invested resources, implemented activities, outputs, outcomes, and long-term goals. Indicators associated with each component are connected through exogenous and endogenous functions, enabling quantitative assessment of the efficiency and effectiveness of MLaaS4H solutions. An illustrative case study demonstrates how coordinated healthcare appointments, public transport services, integrated digital platforms, and rebooking mechanisms can increase access opportunities, reduce temporal mismatches, support vulnerable users, and mitigate private vehicle dependence. While the example addresses passenger mobility, TSMs are equally applicable to freight transport and logistics activities. The proposed framework provides a structured basis for ex ante evaluation and coordinated planning and is intended for researchers in the healthcare and mobility fields, as well as practitioners involved in decision-making and implementation processes.

title: A Large Language Model-Assisted Organizational Decision Support System Integrating Organizational Data with Management Frameworks
abstract: Organizations generate structured and unstructured evidence across workforce activities, projects, assessments, reports, and managerial communication, yet these data are often fragmented across different organizational systems. This study presents IntellicaHR, an Organizational Decision Support System assisted by Large Language Models. The system transforms everyday organizational activities into structured indicators and semantic evidence that can support analysis across organizational and management levels. The McKinsey 7S Framework organizes the collected evidence across key organizational dimensions, whereas Deming&rsquo;s System of Profound Knowledge guides executive-level interpretation. We evaluated the proposed system through three literature-grounded synthetic organizational scenarios, along with supplementary analyses of its semantic-classification and executive-interpretation components. The scenarios produced distinct organizational profiles and role-specific decision-support outputs. An exploratory evaluation of the semantic-classification component showed substantial repeatability, robustness to prompt reformulation, and 95.0% agreement with human-derived sentiment labels, but it was not organization-specific validation. In a blinded human evaluation, 16 participants assessed three alternative executive interpretations: a descriptive Business Intelligence baseline, a generic Large Language Model interpretation, and the proposed Deming-grounded interpretation. The Deming-grounded interpretation received the highest overall ratings and significantly outperformed the Business Intelligence baseline, but not the generic Large Language Model condition. These findings support functional and interpretive coherence without establishing real-world diagnostic validity or organizational effectiveness.

title: Multi-Channel Neighborhood-Constrained Variational Mode Decomposition
abstract: In many multi-channel engineering problems, the information relevant to the task is concentrated in one channel, while the other information plays an auxiliary role. In forecasting, the quantity to be predicted is the primary source of information and the covariates support it; in image processing, the image itself is primary and contextual data are auxiliary. This paper introduces multi-channel neighborhood-constrained variational mode decomposition (NCVMD), an extension of variational mode decomposition (VMD) built on this hierarchy. Where multivariate VMD (MVMD) aligns the modes&rsquo; central frequencies symmetrically and exactly across all channels, NCVMD distinguishes a main channel from auxiliary ones and makes the degree of alignment tunable, reallocating the decomposition error away from the priority channel by a controllable amount. A second contribution is a formal analysis of the resulting optimization problem, which delimits what can be asserted and what cannot. Every subproblem of the alternating scheme is convex and admits a unique closed-form solution, and the main channel provably attains the unconstrained VMD optimum, which MVMD cannot. The joint problem, however, remains nonconvex, so global optimality is not guaranteed. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data confirm the predicted behaviour.

title: SurdoMed: A Morphology-Aware Lexical Mapping and Avatar Architecture for Kazakh Sign Language
abstract: Automatically mapping written Kazakh to dictionary-linked Kazakh Sign Language (KSL) lexical signs is difficult because inflected forms often do not match canonical entries in limited digital lexicons. Surdo Med combines Kazakh natural-language processing, Dimskis notation, reusable avatar animation components, and a web interface for medical-domain lexical learning. This study evaluates morphology-aware lexical concept recovery rather than complete Kazakh-to-KSL translation. The primary benchmark uses naturally occurring inflected tokens from the official UD Kazakh-KTB test split that map uniquely to a frozen medical concept inventory. Across 373 supported inflected tokens, direct lookup recovered 1.61% of target concepts, a rule-based baseline recovered 45.31%, and contextual Stanza lemmatization recovered 97.86% (sentence-cluster bootstrap 95% CI: 96.29&ndash;99.19%). Recovery remained 96.85% after deduplicating surface&ndash;lemma pairs and 94.80% when macro-averaged across 52 lexical concepts. An external analysis using published KSL lexical material showed 20.0% overlap with the medical inventory; within supported items, Stanza recovered 6/6 root tokens versus 3/6 for direct lookup. These results support morphology-aware normalization for dictionary-linked KSL concept recovery. Avatar linguistic quality and educational effectiveness require separate human evaluation.

title: Multi-Objective Security-Aware Workflow Scheduling with Soft Deadlines in Hybrid Clouds
abstract: Hybrid clouds allow service providers to combine secure private resources with elastic public resources, but most schedulers still have three practical limitations: they commonly model task security as a binary constraint, focus on independent tasks rather than dependent workflows, and treat deadlines as hard feasibility constraints rather than service-level objectives with economic penalties. This paper studies multi-objective workflow scheduling in hybrid clouds under multi-level security and soft-deadline constraints. We formulate a multi-objective scheduling problem that captures workflow precedence, heterogeneous private servers and public virtual machines, security-level matching, inter-cloud data transfer, revenue, execution costs, and deadline-violation penalties. We then propose MSWSS, a Multi-level Security-aware Workflow Scheduling with Soft Deadlines algorithm. MSWSS first ranks workflow tasks by deadline pressure, upward rank, security level, and penalty sensitivity; it then filters resources by security clearance; it next selects resources using a profit-aware multi-objective score; and finally it performs local migration and compaction to reduce execution cost and deadline loss. Across 100 independent repetitions at each tested synthetic setting, MSWSS consistently achieves the lowest mean execution cost relative to the three adapted policies, while satisfaction, profit, and deadline violation show setting-dependent trade-offs. In a separate paired default-setting comparison, HEFT obtains slightly better service metrics while MSWSS reduces mean cost by 34.73%. A targeted high-contention ablation further shows that refinement reduces mean cost by 14.12% while decreasing satisfaction and profit and increasing the violation ratio, confirming a cost&ndash;service trade-off rather than universal dominance.

title: A Lightweight Waste Detection Framework with Multi-Scale Feature Fusion and Dynamic Task Alignment for Real-Time Edge Deployment
abstract: Rapid urbanization and continuous population growth have made waste management a critical global challenge. In this study, we construct the Waste4 dataset and propose a lightweight waste detection framework, FLEX-YOLO, to improve detection accuracy and computational efficiency in complex environments. Specifically, an Efficient Multi-Scale Feature Fusion Network (EMBSFPN) is developed to enhance multi-scale feature representation for waste objects with varying scales. The backbone is further enhanced by incorporating MogaBlock into the C3k2 component to improve local&ndash;global feature modeling. Moreover, a Dynamic Task-Aligned Detection Head (DTADH) is introduced to strengthen the interaction between classification and localization through shared feature learning and dynamic alignment strategies. An Efficient Multi-Scale Attention (EMA) mechanism is incorporated before the detection head to suppress background interference and improve target feature discrimination. Experimental results on the Waste4 dataset demonstrate that FLEX-YOLO achieves 97.0% mean Average Precision (mAP) at an Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold of 0.50 (mAP@50) and 74.0% mAP@50&ndash;95. Compared with YOLOv11 and the Real-Time Detection Transformer (RT-DETR), FLEX-YOLO improves mAP@50 by 3.5 and 4.0 percentage points, respectively, and mAP@50&ndash;95 by 3.8 and 3.0 percentage points, respectively. Additional experiments on the Trash Detection Dataset (TDD) show that FLEX-YOLO improves mAP@50 and mAP@50&ndash;95 by 2.2 and 1.9 percentage points, respectively, compared with YOLOv11. Furthermore, deployment on Jetson Orin Nano and Android platforms demonstrates its real-time inference capability and practical applicability. The proposed framework provides an efficient approach for real-world waste detection under resource-constrained edge deployment scenarios.

title: ThyroTrans-XGB: A Hybrid Transformer and Gradient Boosting Framework for Thyroid Disease Classification
abstract: Thyroid disease classification is an important healthcare task because thyroid dysfunction affects metabolism, hormonal balance, cardiovascular activity, and overall well-being. Accurate detection can support timely treatment; however, prediction remains challenging because of nonlinear relationships among biochemical markers, clinical-history variables, missing values, and imbalanced classes. This study proposes ThyroTrans-XGB, a hybrid framework combining Transformer-based feature representation with XGBoost &gt;= 1.0.0 classification. Two publicly available thyroid disease datasets were examined in separate benchmark experiments. The Kaggle Thyroid Disease Dataset was used for binary classification, whereas the UCI Thyroid Disease Dataset was used for a separate multiclass benchmark evaluation. The model was separately trained and evaluated within each dataset-specific setting. The Transformer module learns attention-based representations of thyroid-related variables, while XGBoost performs final classification. Performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, Matthews correlation coefficient, calibration analysis, statistical testing, and SHAP-based explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). ThyroTrans-XGB achieved an F1-score of 0.9828, ROC-AUC of 0.9997, and PR-AUC of 0.9948 on the Kaggle benchmark, and a macro-F1-score of 0.9891, ROC-AUC of 0.9999, and PR-AUC of 0.9928 on the UCI benchmark. Since both datasets were separately trained and evaluated and may share public-data provenance, the UCI experiment represents benchmark evaluation rather than external validation.

title: Mapping Democracy Concepts Through Consensus Clustering of Lexical and Semantic Representations
abstract: Democratic theory encompasses numerous democracy concepts, yet their conceptual relationships are rarely examined systematically at scale. This study develops a reproducible computational framework for grouping 100 democracy concepts from standardized textual descriptions created with large language model (LLM) assistance and verified against source materials. Two complementary representations were constructed: lexical word n-gram term frequency&ndash;inverse document frequency (TF&ndash;IDF) vectors and contextual sentence embeddings. Repeated K-means clustering across multiple random seeds and candidate cluster numbers was summarized through representation-specific co-association matrices and integrated into a consensus similarity matrix. A fifteen-cluster solution, with cluster sizes of 2&ndash;13 concepts and a consensus silhouette of 0.3625, provided the most interpretable balance of stability, granularity, and cluster structure. Lexical and contextual partitions nevertheless overlapped only moderately (mean Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) = 0.22; mean Adjusted Mutual Information (AMI) = 0.34), even though both were derived from the same standardized descriptions. This persistent divergence suggests that short formal textual descriptions capture only part of the semantic structure of democracy concepts. Overall, consensus clustering recovered interpretable macro-families while revealing that complex political concepts cannot be adequately represented by textual similarity alone.

title: An AI-Augmented Decision Architecture for IT Investment: Linking Technical Maturity, Financial Valuation, and Accountable Governance
abstract: Open innovation makes IT investment decisions dependent on knowledge, technologies, and evidence that cross organizational boundaries. Yet these decisions are evaluated through disconnected logics: technical teams assess maturity; executives evaluate cost, strategic value, and flexibility; and artificial intelligence (AI) systems extract evidence or rank alternatives. Their separation creates a translation problem: maturity judgments enter financial models as unexamined assumptions, estimates remain detached from changing technical evidence, and algorithmic recommendations become difficult to contest. This conceptual paper develops the AI-Augmented IT Decision Architecture (AIDA), a closed-loop decision-support architecture connecting an evidence fabric, dynamic maturity assessment, probabilistic valuation, explainable synthesis, and accountable governance. Its design is grounded in a secondary conceptual synthesis of a 39-study core drawn from three previously assembled evidence streams and two post-search updates published in 2026; it is neither a new systematic review nor an empirical validation. AIDA treats evidence bundles, readiness-risk profiles, value-option sets, decision cases, commitment packages, and outcome records as boundary objects coordinating internal and external actors. Twelve propositions specify expected relationships among traceability, uncertainty propagation, option-aware staging, explanation, role separation, feedback, and decision outcomes. The article also contributes a reusable constructed benchmark model: a generative-AI investment case, a fully parameterized 100,000-iteration Monte Carlo implementation, reproducibility files, and a comparative protocol that researchers can reuse, challenge, or extend to evaluate AIDA and alternative approaches. The benchmark demonstrates internal analytical behavior under declared assumptions rather than organizational superiority, while explicit escalation rules distinguish full AIDA from AIDA-Lite. Decision quality is expected to arise not from a single superior method, but from disciplined translation among distributed evidence, economic consequences, and accountable strategic judgment, particularly in open innovation ecosystems where evidence, incentives, and complementary assets span organizational boundaries.

title: Operationalising AI Governance in Public Administration: An Integrated Regulatory and Risk Management Framework
abstract: Public organisations are increasingly using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Algorithmic Decision-making Systems (ADSs), but the rules and governance requirements that apply to them remain spread across different legal and risk-management frameworks. This study analyses the European Union (EU) AI Act, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Directive (EU) 2016/680, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) AI Principles, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) to identify where they overlap, where they differ, and where practical implementation remains difficult. The findings are brought together into an integrated EU framework built around seven governance pillars and eight lifecycle stages, linking regulatory requirements with organisational responsibilities, human oversight, operational controls, and post-deployment monitoring. The framework is illustrated through two public-sector scenarios: social-benefit eligibility and AI-supported student assessment. The analysis shows that governing AI in EU public administration requires more than compliance with individual rules; it requires a coherent process that helps organisations decide when AI is appropriate, who is responsible, what safeguards are needed, and how systems should be reviewed over time. The framework&rsquo;s organisational structure may provide a basis for adaptation to other contexts, but its legal mappings are specific to the EU instruments analysed and would require jurisdiction-specific reconstruction and validation.

title: Resource-Aware Strategic Planning for Partially Observable Star-Sector Tactical Games
abstract: Autonomous agents in adversarial environments must allocate sensing resources, deploy spatial assets, and control combat actions under partial observability. We formulate this coupling as a three-phase partially observable decision process with heterogeneous action spaces. Strategic Planner provides a structured, non-recurrent policy that combines a shared phase-conditioned representation, masked entity attention, a six-channel tactical-map encoder, static plan tokens, competitive entity&ndash;map weighting, and phase-specific heads. Configuration uses a probability-consistent tanh-squashed Gaussian for 11 bounded controls and three categorical choices; deployment and battle use legality-masked categorical distributions. We evaluated the architecture against sequence-aware PPO-GRU and non-recurrent baselines under matched environment-transition budgets. Across eight training seeds, the deterministic win rate was 21.8 &plusmn; 28.0% for Strategic Planner and 25.8 &plusmn; 22.7% for PPO-GRU; their paired difference was &minus;4.0 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [&minus;21.8, 18.1]). Strategic Planner had numerically close mean episode reward (78.0 versus 77.5) and lower mean Command Point cost (753.5 versus 775.9), but paired intervals do not establish an advantage on these endpoints. Peak batch-one GPU allocation was 49.1 versus 54.6 MiB. Three-seed component ablations were inconclusive, and shifted-map outcomes varied. The study delivers an auditable, probability-consistent phase-coupled architecture and a quantified account of its trade-offs with recurrent memory.

title: On-Device Multimodal Small Language Models for Privacy- Preserving Edge Intelligence Through Quantization Pruning Distillation and Energy-Efficient Inference
abstract:
<jats:p>On-device multimodal small language models are emerging as a practical foundation for privacypreserving edge intelligence, enabling devices to interpret and generate language while processing
images, audio, video, sensor streams, and contextual signals without continuous cloud
dependence. Their deployment can reduce data exposure, network latency, connectivity costs, and
centralized infrastructure demand; however, limited memory, compute capability, battery capacity,
thermal headroom, and accelerator support constrain model design and inference. This review
examines architectures, compression techniques, privacy mechanisms, and energy-efficient
inference strategies for multimodal small language models operating on smartphones, wearables,
vehicles, robots, cameras, and embedded Internet of Things platforms. It develops a deploymentcentric taxonomy covering weight, activation, cache, and modality-encoder quantization;
structured, unstructured, token, channel, and modality-aware pruning; response, representation,
cross-modal, and task-specific knowledge distillation; and hybrid compression pipelines. The
review analyzes how these methods affect language quality, visual and acoustic understanding,
cross-modal alignment, robustness, fairness, privacy leakage, memory consumption, latency,
throughput, energy per inference, and thermal stability. Particular attention is given to local
retrieval, adaptive modality selection, speculative decoding, cache management, early exiting,
hardware-aware scheduling, and heterogeneous CPU, GPU, neural, and digital-signal
processing. The paper also evaluates secure personalization, federated updates, trusted execution,
encrypted storage, sensor permission controls, and data-minimizing telemetry. Comparative
evidence is organized by device class, workload, compression target, and evaluation objective. The
gap analysis identifies limited reproducibility, inconsistent energy measurement, weak lowresource language coverage, underdeveloped multimodal privacy benchmarks, and insufficient
study of sustained inference under thermal throttling. It distinguishes theoretical compression
savings from measurable device-level efficiency improvements. The review concludes with
standardized reporting recommendations and research priorities for compact, private, reliable,
and energy-efficient multimodal intelligence at the edge.</jats:p>

title: Empirical Analysis of Small Language Model Quantization for CPU-Only Cloud Infrastructure
evaluatellm: Statistical Inference for Language Model Evaluations
AEGIS: Real-Time Latent-Space Backdoor Detection for Dependable and Secure Small Language Model Inference
abstract: <jats:p>Backdoor attacks pose a serious threat to small language models (SLMs) because compromised models can behave normally on benign inputs while producing attacker-specified outputs when a hidden trigger is activated. Existing defenses commonly require model retraining, operate only before deployment, rely on input-level signals, or incur excessive inference overhead. This paper presents AEGIS (Activation Evaluation and Guardrail for Inference Security), a non-invasive runtime framework for detecting backdoor-induced anomalies in transformer representations. AEGIS dynamically monitors equidistant internal layers, mean-pools and concatenates their hidden states, and compresses the resulting high-dimensional representation into a 64-dimensional latent space. A hybrid compression mechanism uses zero-shot principal component analysis for predominantly linear text representations and a lightweight autoencoder for nonlinear or multimodal representations. Detection is then performed entirely on the GPU using cosine distance from a centroid calibrated on clean data, without modifying or retraining the protected model. We evaluate AEGIS across Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, a 4-bit QLoRA-backdoored Qwen2.5-1.5B model, and a BadNets-backdoored Vision Transformer, covering simulated latent and PEFT-style attacks, genuine fine-tuned backdoors, FP16 inference, and 4-bit NF4 quantization. Across seven experimental scenarios, AEGIS achieves AUROC values between 0.95 and 1.00, true-positive rates between 86% and 100%, and detection latency between 0.47 and 2.40 ms. It obtains AUROC = 1.00 and 100% true-positive rate against the genuinely fine-tuned QLoRA backdoor, while achieving AUROC=0.997 against the fine-tuned visual BadNets attack. Under 4-bit quantization, it retains AUROC=0.95 with 1.50 ms latency and a 4.52 GB memory footprint. These results demonstrate that GPU-native latent-space monitoring can provide effective, retraining-free backdoor detection for real-time transformer inference.</jats:p>

title: AEGIS: Real-Time Latent-Space Backdoor Detection for Dependable and Secure Small Language Model Inference
abstract: <jats:p>Backdoor attacks pose a serious threat to small language models (SLMs) because compromised models can behave normally on benign inputs while producing attacker-specified outputs when a hidden trigger is activated. Existing defenses commonly require model retraining, operate only before deployment, rely on input-level signals, or incur excessive inference overhead. This paper presents AEGIS (Activation Evaluation and Guardrail for Inference Security), a non-invasive runtime framework for detecting backdoor-induced anomalies in transformer representations. AEGIS dynamically monitors equidistant internal layers, mean-pools and concatenates their hidden states, and compresses the resulting high-dimensional representation into a 64-dimensional latent space. A hybrid compression mechanism uses zero-shot principal component analysis for predominantly linear text representations and a lightweight autoencoder for nonlinear or multimodal representations. Detection is then performed entirely on the GPU using cosine distance from a centroid calibrated on clean data, without modifying or retraining the protected model. We evaluate AEGIS across Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, a 4-bit QLoRA-backdoored Qwen2.5-1.5B model, and a BadNets-backdoored Vision Transformer, covering simulated latent and PEFT-style attacks, genuine fine-tuned backdoors, FP16 inference, and 4-bit NF4 quantization. Across the main optimized shield-overhead experiments, AEGIS achieves AUROC values between 0.95 and 1.00, true-positive rates between 86% and 100%, and prefill-stage detection latency between 0.47 and 2.40 ms. In the dedicated T4 deployment stress tests, which measure the full guardrail overhead under edge and real QLoRA settings, latency ranges from 5.20 to 7.77 ms with combined model-plus-guardrail memory between 2.59 and 4.02 GB. AEGIS obtains AUROC = 1.00 and 100% true-positive rate against the genuinely fine-tuned QLoRA backdoor, while achieving AUROC = 0.997 against the fine-tuned visual BadNets attack. Under 4-bit quantization, it retains an AUROC = 0.95 with a 4.02 GB memory footprint. These results show that a compact GPU-native implementation of activation-space monitoring can provide effective, retraining-free backdoor detection for real-time transformer inference.</jats:p>

title: Mixed-Precision Logarithmic Quantization for Efficient Neural Network Inference on FPGAs_supp1-3730233.mp4
DVFS for Small Language Model Inference on Mobile Edge Devices
TRIAD: Co-designing mixed-precision quantization, operator fusion, and on-chip memory reuse for real-time vision–language–action inference on automotive NPUs

Quantization Techniques for Efficient Inference of
Large Language Models
abstract:
<jats:p>Our research presents a comprehensive evaluation of quantization techniques applied to
transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs). We investigate Post-Training Quantization
(PTQ), Quantization-Aware Training (QAT), ultra-low-precision methods (INT4, INT3) and mixedprecision strategies. Practical experiments are conducted using toolchains such as Hugging Face
Transformers, AutoGPTQ and BitsAndBytes to quantize and deploy models like GPT-2, LLaMA 2
(7B) and Mistral (7B). Runtime performance, memory footprint and output quality are compared
across full-precision (FP16/FP32) and quantized (INT8/INT4) versions under consistent input and
inference settings. Our results show that quantization offers substantial performance gains, up to
40% faster inference.</jats:p>

title: Runtime Adaptive FPGA Architecture for Dynamic Language Model Inference in Intelligent Vehicles
abstract: <jats:p>Runtime adaptive FPGA execution is attractive for in-vehicle language models because the dominant bottleneck changes with context length, inference phase, and memory pressure. This work develops a ZCU102/XCZU9EG-oriented architecture with four constant-budget modes that redistribute 2,048 DSPs between attention and feed-forward processing under a stateful break-even controller. Evaluation combines checkpoint-level W8A8 screening, benchmark-derived automotive request statistics, analytical and event models, and Monte Carlo controller experiments. For SmolLM2-135M-Instruct, W8A8 screening increases WikiText-2 perplexity by 2.95%; 390,510 STRIDE-QA human turns have a median length of 14 tokens and p95 of 48. The compute model predicts an attention-heavy-mode benefit of 22.01% at 8,192 tokens. Across twenty independent 1,000-request traces per workload, the controller reduces mean modeled request latency by 1.68% for routine traffic, 16.75% for multimodal traffic, and 17.49% for long-context bursts relative to static C0. Executed W8A8 operator tests report 1.38–1.77% normalized RMSE and cosine similarity above 0.99984. These results support context-aware, transition-cost-aware resource allocation for adaptive edge language-model acceleration.</jats:p>

title: Capability, ranking dynamics, and inference pricing in the large language model ecosystem: evidence from linked public data
abstract: Public leaderboards and pricing catalogues offer complementary but hard-to-combine views of the large language model ecosystem. We analyse three linked public sources: an archived Open LLM Leaderboard v2 sample of 4,565 open-weight evaluation records with complete six-benchmark scores; an 89-snapshot human-preference panel of 279 models (June 2024–August 2025); and 2,685 priced chat endpoints (October 2026). Principal component analysis identifies a dominant common component (74% of benchmark variance), retained by parallel analysis and robust to family deduplication. Benchmark performance rises with parameter count (13.6 points per tenfold) and with submission date at constant size and type (10.5 points per year) under family-clustered inference. A documented change of the default rating on 20 May 2025 shifted all listed scores by about 18 points; within the stable period the preference frontier rose by about 187 points per year relative to a fixed reference set through 17 leaders with median spells of 12 days, top-20 slots concentrated among fewer organisations, and ratings did not drift within models. Among 201 models listed by three or more providers, the median maximum-to-minimum price ratio is 1.38 (1.27 under version-strict identifiers). A hedonic model adjusting for time since first listing attributes multipliers of about 3.1 to one standard deviation of arena score and 0.18 to open-weight status, robust to version-exact matching. Preference ratings and benchmark averages agree strongly for 69 matched models. Temporal mismatch, selective coverage, and related model families preclude causal interpretation.

title: Quantization-Induced Accuracy Degradation in Small Language Models: A Parametric Scaling Analysis
OBLIVION TextLM: A Query-relative Control Plane for Efficient Generative Language-model Inference
abstract: <jats:p>Long-context language models can ingest far more information than a particular query actually requires, yet retaining every represented distinction is neither equivalent to using it well nor automatically computationally efficient. We present OBLIVION TextLM, a model-agnostic query-relative control plane that operationalizes unresolved semantic obligations around a separately licensed pretrained language-model executor. The system constructs a live obligation state, routes evidence against that state, invokes the executor, permits new obligations to be born from intermediate evidence, generates evidence-bound completion certificates, verifies discharge conservatively, and retires an obligation only when verification and an explicit net-gain audit both succeed. Three matched modes—full-context baseline, retrieval-augmented generation, and OBLIVION—use the same executor to separate foundation-model quality from retrieval and control effects. The v2.0.0 reference implementation adds hybrid routing, citations, memory, streaming OpenAI-compatible clients, verifier separation, tracing, usage accounting, benchmarking, safety utilities, and advisory KV-cache ownership hooks. We validate the artifact by compilation, 29 automated tests, release-metadata checks, and deterministic three-mode smoke runs. We deliberately distinguish text-level semantic retirement from unmeasured physical KV-cache or GPU savings. The contribution is an executable, falsifiable systems framework for testing when verified query-relative state control improves quality–compute trade-offs without claiming a separately trained foundation model of its own.</jats:p>

title: Algorithmic Virtual Inertia: Dynamic Quantization of LLM Inference for Fast Frequency Response via Stochastic Impulse Control
abstract: <jats:p>As gigawatt-scale AI workloads strain low-inertia grids, traditional demand response fails to address stability crises due to critical timescale mismatches. This paper introduces Joule-per-Token Arbitrage, a stochastic control framework treating inference precision as a liquid control variable capable of sub-cycle actuation. We formulate the grid-compute nexus as a Stochastic Hybrid System (SHS), deriving an optimal control policy via Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Quasi-Variational Inequalities (HJB-QVI) to financialize Large Language Model (LLM) accuracy. Unlike binary load-shedding, our framework modulates GPU quantization states (FP16 → INT8 → INT4) to shed power with 16 ms latency while maintaining service continuity. Validated via a 2021 ERCOT Winter Storm Uri Digital Twin, simulations demonstrate a 1 GW AI cluster stabilizes frequency nadir 3× faster than conventional inertia (improving nadir from 59.30 Hz to 59.52 Hz). This prevents Tier-1 load shedding and reduces Rate-of-Change-of-Frequency (RoCoF) by 33%, with <5% transient perplexity increase. This work quantifies the thermodynamic exchange between computational intelligence and grid inertia, providing a pathway for gigawatt-scale virtual synchronous machines derived from algorithmic flexibility.</jats:p>

title: QAQ: Query-Adaptive Quantization for Large Language Model Inference
Hardware-Assisted Dynamic Quantization for Low-Power DNN Inference on Edge FPGAs
abstract: <jats:p>Energy efficiency poses a significant challenge when deploying Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) on resource-constrained Edge AI hardware. Traditional quantization strategies often rely on a fixed bit-width during execution, creating a rigid trade-off between energy consumption, latency, and network accuracy. To tackle this issue, we introduce a hardware-assisted dynamic quantization control framework leveraging a Hardware/Software Co-Design approach, capable of dynamic precision scaling across a wide spectrum from 16-bit down to 2-bit. By implementing a lightweight ingress FIFO buffer at the FPGA hardware level, the system observes input stream congestion in real time and autonomously orchestrates precision-control signals on the fly, mitigating simulated buffer backlog and suppressing frame drops during burst traffic scenarios. A hysteresis-damped hardware finite state machine (FSM) controller is integrated to ensure operational stability without host-CPU intervention. Experimental evaluation via PyTorch-based co-simulation alongside physical hardware synthesis on an AMD Xilinx Zynq-7000 FPGA (Digilent ZedBoard) using the German Traffic Sign Recognition Benchmark (GTSRB) demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves 94.35% ± 0.05% Top-1 accuracy across five independent evaluation runs, matching the 16-bit baseline within 0.02 pp, while dynamically relieving queue pressure. Furthermore, the dedicated control-plane logic incurs a low resource footprint utilizing less than 0.01% of FPGA logic resources (three LUTs and one Flip-Flop) and a standalone dynamic power of 7.0 mW (projected to <1.0 mW for core logic in integrated SoCs), providing an autonomous, low-overhead supervisory control mechanism for adaptive edge inference.</jats:p>

title: Adapting a small language model for plant protection information in Türkiye
abstract: Plant protection advice must connect biological knowledge with product use, legal conditions, and evidence from sources. A fluent answer can omit a restriction or confuse a residue limit with permission to use a product. Small language models offer a practical route to local information services. However, local model training does not show that agricultural advice is reliable. This study examines BitkiKorumacı, a Turkish system that combines a source database with adaptation of a small language model. Four development configurations use a four-bit Qwen3 model with four billion parameters and low-rank adaptation. The analysis compares archived answers with and without added database evidence. It covers 860 cases across 14 task categories. Developers repeatedly used this evaluation set, so the results describe development performance. The B2S configuration passed the automatic answer criterion on 112 of 860 cases without added retrieval and 601 cases with retrieval. These results correspond to 13.02% and 69.88%. B2S with added retrieval met 12 of 14 category thresholds. It still failed the resistance task, the source-based examination task, and separate behavior checks. All four configurations still had behavior failures. All 1,000 benchmark cases lack completed independent expert review. The campaign revised 285 references as passage-based assistant drafts. In passage tasks, added retrieval did not improve the pooled score. Most of the overall increase occurred in categories that received extra database context. The results show that local adaptation can improve the use of supplied evidence within this task design. They do not show field accuracy or the safety of autonomous advice. The study gives a documented development case for Turkish plant protection and lists the tests necessary before practical use.

title: Towards Efficient Vision-Language Model Inference via Stepwise Visual Token Pruning
abstract: <jats:p>Vision-Language Models (VLMs) generate hundreds to thousands of visual tokens per image, making token-dependent computation across decoder layers, including projection, FFN, and attention, as well as KV-cache memory, a major inference bottleneck. Existing token pruning methods address this issue in two ways. Pre-decoder pruning shortens the input sequence but cannot account for the textual query, whereas in-decoder pruning enables query-aware selection but retains the full token cost in early decoder layers. We show that these two strategies are structurally complementary and propose a training-free two-stage framework that exploits this complementarity through stepwise token reduction. In the first stage, CaNS (CLS-Attention Neighbor Selection) performs spatially coherent pre-decoder pruning to shorten the sequence while preserving salient regions. In the second stage, DaFT (Dual-Attention Filtered Token Pruning) refines visual tokens within the decoder usinga V2T→T2V dual-attention mechanism for query-conditioned selection. On LLaVA-1.5, our method reduces 576 visual tokens to 32, a 94.4% reduction, while retaining 97.1% of the baseline performance and reducing FLOPs to 27.9% of the baseline decoder cost, or 37.8% of the full-model cost including the vision encoder. It also generalizes to LLaVA-NeXT, achieving up to a 3.00× speedup under aggressive compression.</jats:p>

title: Quantization of Complementary ADHM Sigma Model
abstract: <jats:p>We discuss quantization of complementary ADHM sigma model in parallel with the quantization of the Witten&apos;s original ADHM sigma model by Lambert. The mechanisms of divergence cancellation in two models are different from each other.</jats:p>

title: Reusing obsolete windows 10 PCs for on-premises large language model inference
abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The Windows 10 end-of-life provides a material incentive to repurpose legacy PCs as on-premises large language model (LLM) inference servers. This study assesses the technical feasibility, economic viability and the environmental and social issues of converting an enterprise workstation with an NVIDIA Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) into a dedicated AI node. Using Proxmox virtualisation, Ollama, and Open WebUI to benchmark several open-source LLMs, this study shows that a repurposed workstation, fitted with a single consumer-grade NVIDIA GPU, can deliver stable inference throughput of 29–65 tokens/s for bounded, conversational coding and document-assistant workflows, while preserving full data sovereignty and eliminating recurring subscription fees. Performance analysis reveals that resource contention and GPU memory allocation are the primary determinants of throughput. Correctness, assessed against three established public benchmarks with gold answers, does not track the same ranking as throughput; combining both axes identifies gemma4:e4b as the strongest model evaluated on this hardware for both speed and correctness, while the slowest model tested was among the most accurate. A cost-benefit model shows local operation is substantially cheaper than mid-range and premium cloud alternatives, and only modestly costlier than the cheapest cloud tier on a per-prompt basis—a gap this study argues is outweighed by the digital-sovereignty benefits of local control, particularly where compliance-driven data-handling constraints apply. The study summarizes key background motivations for on-premises AI—privacy, security, regulatory risk—and estimates that this repurposed workstation's usage-phase
                    <jats:italic>CO</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    e footprint is lower than each of the cloud alternatives compared, in addition to avoiding the embodied manufacturing emissions of new hardware. Repurposing legacy workstations with readily available open source tools offers a sustainable, cost-effective pathway for organizations to deploy practical LLM inference capabilities locally, providing a strategic alternative to cloud services for entities that prioritize privacy, regulatory compliance or long-term cost containment.
                  </jats:p>

title: Post-Training Low-Bit Quantization for Edge-Sensor Neural Inference
TMXVAR: Twin Microscaling Floating-Point Quantization for Efficient Visual Autoregressive Model Inference on FPGA
Neuro-Fetcher: An Asynchronous Learning-Based Key-Value Cache Pre-fetching Pipeline for Efficient Large Language Model Inference
abstract: <jats:p>The immense size of the Key-Value (KV) cache in Large Language Models (LLMs) has made autoregressive inference a significant memory-bandwidth bottleneck. Recent KV cache compression methods mainly utilize handcraft or heuristic rules to pre-fetch the important KV cache entries and emit unnecessary caches. These rule-based methods fail to capture the complex dynamic attention patterns inherent in different models and data distributions, leading to degradation of downstream tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel learning-based KV cache management approach named Neuro-Fetcher, which is a lightweight neural network trained to accurately predict important KV cache entries by the relationship between input tokens and intermediate attention patterns. This learning-based pre-fetching strategy can improve the accuracy of KV cache prediction and the performance of downstream tasks. Our work overcomes two critical challenges for learning-based pre-fetchers: we propose the "Shallow Pre-fetching" strategy to tackle the high complexity of multi-layer prediction, and design a "Ping-Pong Scheduling" mechanism to effectively hide the inference latency of the predictor itself. The experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves inference throughput over strong heuristic baselines without compromising model perplexity. Furthermore, we conduct an analysis of the model generalization capabilities and demonstrate that our Neuro-Fetcher could exhibit strong zero-shot intra-family transferability (e.g., OPT-13B to OPT-6.7B), unlocking a &apos;train-once, deploy-anywhere within the family&apos; paradigm that drastically reduces deployment costs.</jats:p>

title: Fully Quantized Training vs. Post-Training Quantization for a Small Hyperspectral Transformer Model for Pixel-Level Foreign Plastic Object Classification
abstract: <jats:p>Low-precision floating-point computation has become central to efficient artificial intelligence, yet its behavior for compact transformer-based hyperspectral imaging (HSI) models remains underexplored. In this work, we present a controlled comparative study of fully quantized training (FQT) and post-training quantization (PTQ) for pixel-wise foreign plastic object (FPO) classification in poultry hyperspectral data. Using a fixed state-of-the-art spatial–spectral transformer backbone, a common mixed-precision strategy, and identical training and inference protocols, we evaluate FP32, FP16, BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 across predictive performance, model compression, training efficiency, and inference efficiency. The results show that mixed-precision FQT remains highly robust across the tested precision spectrum, with all reduced-precision configurations staying within 0.63 percentage points of the FP32 baseline in overall accuracy while consistently outperforming PTQ at matched precisions. Across the evaluated formats, BF16 provides the closest accuracy to FP32, whereas FP8 offers a particularly favorable balance between accuracy preservation and reduced precision, while model compression increases progressively to 3.69× under NVFP4. The computational benefits, however, are strongly workload dependent. Native FP8/FP4 hardware support does not automatically improve training throughput for this compact model at moderate workloads, and the larger training batches required to better utilize low-precision hardware can degrade predictive performance. In contrast, large-batch inference can effectively exploit FP8 and NVFP4 without affecting predictive accuracy. An ablation study further shows that selective retention of numerically sensitive modules in FP32 is essential for stable ultra-low-precision operation. Overall, the findings demonstrate that low precision is a viable but workload-dependent design choice for compact HSI transformers, with FQT providing greater accuracy robustness than PTQ and FP8, offering a favorable overall accuracy–efficiency trade-off.</jats:p>

title: Characterizing KV-Cache Performance in Large Language Model Inference: Context Length, Attention Architecture, and GPU Memory Residency
abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) commonly employ key–value (KV) caching to avoid recomputing previous attention states during autoregressive inference. However, its measured performance benefit depends on workload characteristics and the memory environment. This study presents a controlled systems characterization of KV-cache performance across input context length, grouped-query attention configurations, and GPU-memory residency. Experiments use Qwen2.5-3B and SmolLM3-3B under verified fully resident conditions with fixed 128-token generation, prompt lengths from 128 to 2048 tokens, randomized cache-enabled/cache-disabled execution, GPU telemetry, and repeated paired validation. KV-cache speedup increases from 1.34× to 8.31× for Qwen2.5-3B and from 1.28× to 8.62× for SmolLM3-3B. At 2048 prompt tokens, 30 randomized paired trials confirm mean speedups of 8.10× and 8.51×, corresponding to runtime reductions of 87.65% and 88.25%, while physical GPU-memory utilization remains below 61%. Despite SmolLM3-3B requiring twice the theoretical KV-cache storage per token, both models show comparable context-dependent scaling in the fully resident regime. A separate Mistral-7B case study further demonstrates that memory pressure can substantially alter apparent speedup. These results establish KV-cache speedup as workload- and system-dependent and demonstrate that meaningful benchmarking requires reporting context length, cache configuration, model and cache footprints, physical accelerator-memory residency, runtime, throughput, and relevant GPU-memory conditions during each inference experiment.</jats:p>

title: Dynamic Semantic Adaptation for Efficient Large Language Model Inference
A Survey on Quantization Techniques for Large Language Models
abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across modern language tasks, but their significant computational and memory demands make them difficult to deploy on limited hardware. To overcome this, quantization—reducing numerical precision from 32-bit to lower-bit formats such as 4-bit—has emerged as an effective compression method to minimize model size and enhance inference efficiency. The objective of this paper is to review recent advancements in LLM quantization, outline the key challenges involved, and examine how different techniques attempt to address them. This review is based on a focused analysis of recent peer-reviewed studies and introduces a high-level taxonomy of modern methods, complemented by a comparative performance summary to illustrate their practical impact. Comparative analysis across selected papers highlights that quantization effectively reduces model size and memory consumption while maintaining near-original accuracy and significant inference speedups. In conclusion, modern quantization techniques strike an optimal balance between accuracy, efficiency, and resource utilization, enabling scalable and affordable deployment of large-scale AI models across diverse computing platforms.</jats:p>

title: Efficient Reasoning at the Edge: A Systematic Review of Small Reasoning Models, Test-Time Scaling, Quantization, and Energy-Aware AI Inference
Canonical and Compact Representations in Small Language Model Graph Classification
abstract: <jats:p>Small language models can classify graphs serialized as text, but three properties of graphs complicate the conversion: a graph has no intrinsic vertex order, so one graph yields many texts; explicit serializations are long under a fixed input budget; and one serialization shows only a single view of the structure. We evaluate the corresponding design responses under one protocol. Raw adjacency and edge lists are compared with a degree-sorted ordering, two exact canonical serializations, a deterministic BFS profile, compact Graph6 and NetLSD encodings, soft-prompt baselines, and validation-weighted late fusion. On five TUDataset benchmarks and three instruction-tuned small language models, the exact canonical serializations improve over raw adjacency lists in 14 of the 15 settings, and late fusion improves on that baseline in all 15. The compact encodings shorten the input by 67.7% and 42.2%, respectively, and both exceed the baseline in mean accuracy. A paired analysis with correction for multiple comparisons confirms the gain for both canonical serializations, the deterministic profile, the degree-sorted ordering, NetLSD, and late fusion. Serialization is therefore a consequential modeling decision, not merely a preprocessing step. This study provides an empirical basis for that decision by measuring accuracy, permutation robustness, input length, and preprocessing cost under a single protocol.</jats:p>

title: REFINE-Verilog: Reliability-Based Fine-Tuning and Inference Enhancement for Small Language Model in Partial Verilog Generation
Enabling Efficient Serverless Inference Serving for LLM (Large Language Model) in the Cloud
abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">This review report examines the problem of cold-start latency in serverless inference for large language models (LLMs) and surveys recent systems that address it, with a particular focus on ServerlessLLM. In serverless environments, loading multi-hundred-gigabyte LLM checkpoints and initializing GPU resources can dominate end-to-end latency, making real-time applications such as conversational agents and translation services difficult to deploy cost-efficiently. The report first summarizes the cold-start problem and common mitigation strategies in today's Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) platforms, including container warming, host-side checkpoint caching, and cluster-level storage servers. It then reviews the design of ServerlessLLM, which exploits underutilized multi-tier storage in GPU servers, a loading-optimized checkpoint format, live inference migration based on token-level state transfer, and a startup-time-aware model scheduler. Additional methods from recent literature, such as RainbowCake's layered container caching, and the cold-start handling mechanisms of major cloud providers are also discussed. Drawing on the evaluation presented in the original work, the report highlights that multi-tier checkpoint loading and live migration reduce model startup time by up to 6-8× compared to conventional formats, and deliver up to 28× lower startup latency than Ray Serve for large models in realistic traces. The review concludes by outlining open challenges and future directions, including integrating model compression, multi-level inference pipelines, and advanced memory-offloading techniques to further improve the scalability and efficiency of serverless LLM inference.</jats:p>

Hallucination Mitigation in Large Language Models: A Review and Exploratory Small-Model Pilot
abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) can produce fluent responses that are false, unsupported, outdated, or more certain than the available evidence justifies. This manuscript presents a narrative review of major hallucination-mitigation approaches and an exploratory pilot intended to refine a future evaluation protocol rather than establish model-level performance. The review covers false-premise handling, abstention and knowledge-boundary estimation, retrieval-augmented generation, grounding, verification, self-checking, and multimodal hallucination. It also distinguishes published evidence from an engineering proposal for failure-driven correction. The pilot used a locally executed interface labeled Gemma 3 1B-IT and ten hand-designed stress prompts spanning false premises, insufficient evidence, fabricated-citation traps, unknowable events, and future-value requests. The revised analysis deliberately avoids compressing these observations into a single hallucination score. Two responses were epistemically appropriate, three were partially appropriate but introduced unsupported content, and five failed the target behavior. Generation stability was tracked separately: one otherwise appropriate answer entered a repetition loop, and another item required a restart after a context-length error. An extended follow-up run was terminated when the local system became unstable and began returning empty outputs; those observations are reported only qualitatively. The pilot is too small and insufficiently controlled to support causal claims or generalization to the Gemma family. Its value is methodological: it illustrates why hallucination research should report multiple axes - factual correctness, false-premise resistance, correct abstention, unnecessary abstention, grounding fidelity, coverage, calibration where available, and generation stability - rather than one aggregate number. The literature further suggests that mitigation is most credible when model behavior, external evidence, verification, and evaluation design are treated as a coupled system.</jats:p>

MindCore: A Safety-Gated, Memory-Augmented Small Language Model Architecture for Culturally Adapted Mental Wellness Support in India
abstract: <jats:p>Mental health support in India faces a large treatment gap, and small language models (SLMs) are attractive for low-cost wellness applications but raise open questions about safety, memory and clinical validity. We describe MindCore, a wellness-support system built around a LoRA-adapted Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct model, and a control architecture that wraps the model with three components: (i) a deterministic multilingual crisis gate that bypasses the model and returns helpline information; (ii) a conversational administration of the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 questionnaires, framed strictly as self-assessment and not diagnosis; and (iii) a three-layer memory (working, episodic, semantic) with exact timestamps that lets the system recall earlier sessions after days or months. We evaluate the components that do not require GPU inference on author-constructed test sets (36 crisis and 33 non-crisis messages in English, Hinglish and Hindi; 26 focus-classification items; 39 questionnaire answers; 20 synthetic users). The first version only labelled crisis language without acting on it and flagged 7 of 26 explicit crisis statements (26.9%). The gated version flagged 23 of 26 (88.5%) and, after a patch made in response to the observed failures, 26 of 26 on the same development set, but flagged none of 10 indirect expressions of hopelessness (95% CI 0-28%). Testing also exposed defects such as scoring "I don't know" as "not at all". Keyword memory retrieval reached 80% Hit@3 for lexically matching queries but 50% for paraphrases, close to a 40% recency-only baseline. The language model was not evaluated end to end, no human participants were involved, and no clinical validity is claimed. We discuss limitations, regulatory and privacy considerations, and a roadmap toward clinician-reviewed evaluation.</jats:p>
